articles.title: Elephants use medicinal plants to treat themselves, researchers find
articles.summary: African elephants use dozens of different medicinal plants to treat themselves and their families when they are sick, research reveals.
articles.content:
The scientists collaborated with the conservation charity the Mount Elgon Foundation, external. They interviewed local people, including wildlife scouts and community elders.

Accounts described elephants selecting particular plants when they seemed unwell, and mothers reportedly giving medicinal plant material to their calves.

From this, the researchers concluded that the elephants use 35 different plant species, and that 25 of those are known locally to have medicinal uses.

The study, published in the journal Scientific Reports, external, did not name the interviewees - keeping participants anonymous so they felt free to share their stories.

Their accounts reveal some intriguing details. In one testimony, a wildlife scout described seeing elephants using a plant known as Angurweet "as medicine to give to babies".

Angurweet is used as a remedy for ailments including stomach ache. The scout, who described elephant mothers mixing it in their mouths - "removing the leaves and chewing it until smooth, along with the roots of some other trees".

He also recounted that he had seen mothers mix this plant material with their own milk. "They give it to the babies, who chew on it themselves and spit out the solids".

Professor Michael Huffman, a primatologist based in Japan, currently at Nagasaki University, said this particular account was "tantalising", but more evidence would be needed to prove that elephants provided bespoke medical treatment for their calves.

The scientists have already embarked on gathering that evidence - giving the local wildlife experts they worked with cameras to record the behaviour they witness.

They are also analysing plants that the elephants use - looking for new medicines that the elephants themselves may have discovered.

Another lead reearcher on the project, Dr Fabien Schultz from the Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine in Hamburg, told BBC News: "Local knowledge has given us a map".

"We [now] want to follow the elephants and investigate whether they select particular plants in particular health contexts, and whether those plants have relevant biological activity."
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery about African elephants using medicinal plants for self-treatment, revealing animal intelligence and traditional ecological knowledge. This has broad implications for conservation, biodiversity understanding, and potential medical discoveries benefiting society. The story is well-focused, detailed, and highlights ongoing research with meaningful environmental and scientific impact.

articles.title: NASA’s Machines for Mars Make Beer Bubbly
articles.summary: Carbon-capture technology repurposed for breweries spreads and finds new applications
articles.content:
A brewer makes adjustments to the Earthly Labs carbon-capture unit, which purifies carbon dioxide from the beer brewing process for use in carbonation. Credit: Chart Industries Inc.

In 2021, Maine Beer Company’s carbon dioxide supplier ran short on carbon dioxide.

“There was potential for our beer to go stale in the tanks,” said Dave Love, the brewery’s sustainability manager. “We wouldn’t be able to use CO 2 for any of our bottling, kegging, or centrifuge operations.”

The solution the company settled on originated on Mars — or more specifically, in NASA’s plans for harvesting resources from the Red Planet. Now it’s saving money and reducing emissions for wineries, distilleries, power companies, helium producers, and more.

Beginning in the 1990s, the company Pioneer Astronautics won multiple Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) contracts from Johnson Space Center in Houston to build systems that could generate resources on Mars. The technology could, for example, capture carbon dioxide from the Martian atmosphere and combine it with hydrogen to produce water for life support and methane for rocket fuel. These capabilities weren’t entirely new, but Pioneer’s systems were compact, efficient, and automated.

Later, Pioneer Astronautics founder Robert Zubrin created Pioneer Energy to rearrange these subsystems into technology for the oil and gas industry (Spinoff 2015, 2020). He soon realized technology for capturing and purifying carbon dioxide on Mars could do the same in a brewery, capturing CO 2 from the brewing process for use in carbonation. By 2015, the Craft Brewery Recovery System was in production (Spinoff 2016). In the end, though, the company put the system up for licensing.

Amy George founded Earthly Labs of Austin, Texas, in 2016 to develop small-scale carbon capture. She discovered the Craft Brewery Recovery System and obtained an exclusive license.

Since the pandemic reduced its availability, carbon dioxide has continued experiencing shortages and volatility, and George said these have emerged as major drivers of interest in the technology.

And it isn’t just helping brewers. After expanding into wineries and distilleries, Earthly Labs started discovering other markets. Energy companies often generate carbon dioxide as a by-product, which they can sell if it’s captured. Several are now customers.

Another application finding new customers is helium production. Helium, which is used to make microchips and fiber-optic cables, among other applications, is found in underground deposits, mixed with other gases, such as methane and carbon dioxide, that need to be separated.

In 2021, Earthly Labs was acquired by Chart Industries Inc., which specializes in cryogenic equipment engineering and has helped scale up the technology for applications like power plants.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a real-world application of NASA-developed carbon-capture technology originally intended for Mars, now repurposed to reduce carbon emissions and improve sustainability in breweries, wineries, distilleries, and other industries. This technology addresses carbon dioxide shortages and supports environmental benefits by capturing and reusing CO2, with expanding impact across multiple sectors. The story is focused, detailed, and highlights a significant positive environmental innovation with broad societal benefits.

**What happened** – A company called Pioneer Astronautics adapted this Mars technology for Earth industries. By 2015, they created a system to capture CO2 from beer brewing, which helps reuse the gas to carbonate beer. Later, Earthly Labs, a startup in Texas, licensed this system and improved it. Since 2021, after being bought by Chart Industries, the technology has spread to wineries, distilleries, power plants, and helium producers.

**Impact** – This technology helps solve CO2 shortages that breweries and other industries face. Instead of buying CO2, they capture and clean the gas produced during their processes to use again. This lowers costs and reduces emissions. It also helps companies that produce gases like helium separate them more efficiently. The technology originally made for Mars is now helping many Earth industries become more sustainable.

**What’s next step** – Chart Industries is working to scale up the technology so more industries can benefit. As demand for CO2 and helium grows, this carbon-capture system could become a standard tool for reducing waste and cutting emissions in multiple sectors.

**One-sentence takeaway** – NASA’s Mars carbon-capture technology is now helping breweries and other industries recycle CO2, saving money and protecting the environment.

articles.title: Ethiopia’s Green Legacy Initiative is turning citizens into foresters
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM For most of the past century, Ethiopia was losing its forests. From the turn of the millennium to 2025, the country shed 560,000 hectares, about 2,160 square miles, of tree cover to agriculture, logging, and charcoal fuel. Then the government launched the Green Legacy Initiative in 2019, and citizens […]
The post Ethiopia’s Green Legacy Initiative is turning citizens into foresters first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

For most of the past century, Ethiopia was losing its forests. From the turn of the millennium to 2025, the country shed 560,000 hectares, about 2,160 square miles, of tree cover to agriculture, logging, and charcoal fuel. Then the government launched the Green Legacy Initiative in 2019, and citizens started planting trees. A lot of them. A lot of trees.

The official numbers raise questions. The government claims to have planted 48 billion trees in seven years, including a reported 353 million seedlings in a single day. The goal is 50 billion by 2030, but researchers who have reviewed Ethiopian tree-planting programs found that 10 of 15 schemes with set targets achieved less than 50 percent success. Studies in Asia suggest nearly half of all reforestation trees don’t survive five years. The government’s own technical committee put Ethiopia’s rates at 83 percent survival in 2019 and 79 percent the year after; some researchers have questioned those figures, and a more systematic independent assessment is now underway.

Yitebitu Moges, who coordinates the UN Environment Programme’s REDD+ deforestation scheme in Ethiopia, acknowledges the uncertainty but doesn’t think it undermines what’s happening. “Even if half of the trees that have been planted survive, we are already gaining moisture, keeping soil and sequestering carbon,” he says. The change he cares about most is harder to measure: “Our history has shifted from deforestation to forestation. People are becoming more and more aware that deforestation is damaging.”

The woman who proved her neighbors wrong

In the Berbere district of Oromia, Halima Kedir started planting trees and kept going despite her neighbors’ doubts. “They thought I was striving for nothing,” she says, sitting in a garden now full of banana, olive, and grevillea. She has planted thousands of trees and lost count of exactly how many. The results changed minds that were once firmly against her.

Her neighbor Fate Abdulahi, once among the skeptics, now calls her “a role model and someone willing to find local solutions to our issues.”

Kedir, 35, describes her relationship with the seedlings through guddifachaa, the Oromo tradition of adopting children into family and community. “Just like we adopt a child in our tradition, I see them like my own children,” she says. The area has severe water shortages. She walks about an hour each way to fetch water for her trees. Her 13-year-old son, Anwar Hassen, says he wants to “make a lifelong commitment in the fight against climate change.”

Thousands of households in the area have joined the initiative. WaterAid Ethiopia has distributed approximately 55,000 indigenous tree seedlings across the district, with an 85 percent growth rate reported so far.

Behind the 50 billion number

Ethiopia’s annual deforestation rate fell from 92,000 hectares (about 227,000 acres) in 2013 to 27,703 hectares (roughly 68,500 acres) in 2023, a drop of roughly 70 percent. Forest cover rose from 15.5 to 23.6 percent over the same period.

Those numbers come from the government. Independent verification of long-term survival rates is still in progress, and how many of the 48 billion claimed trees are still alive has not been established from outside. Moges says a systematic study is now collecting that data. His own view: whether the survival rate turns out to be 50 percent or 80 percent, Ethiopia is already holding more soil, retaining more moisture, and storing more carbon than it was. The gap in the numbers doesn’t cancel out the changes on the ground.

In 2024, the Ethiopian parliament set up the Green Legacy and Landscape Restoration Special Fund, allocating between 0.5 and 1 percent of the annual federal budget, roughly $63 million to $140 million, to restoring degraded land.

From Berbere to Addis Ababa to COP32

In November 2027, Ethiopia will host COP32, the 32nd UN climate summit, in Addis Ababa. Part of the reason is what the country has been doing with its trees. Kedir, tending seedlings in Berbere, already has a message ready for whoever shows up. “They should give the issues of water and trees, which many in such communities lack, the priority they deserve,” she says.

Teshome Soromessa, an environmentalist at Addis Ababa University, says the initiative has brought communities, universities, civil society, and government around a shared goal. Most of it started the same way: someone deciding to plant something and not stopping.

Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary.

articles.title: The tilcayo: new wildcat species discovered in Bolivia’s cloud forest
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM For years, biologists cataloguing Bolivia’s Yungas cloud forest would note a small spotted cat and move on. Tiger cat, broadly speaking. The general profile fit and there was no obvious reason to dig further. Local communities had always called it something different. Tilcayo, a name that treated this animal […]
The post The tilcayo: new wildcat species discovered in Bolivia’s cloud forest first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

For years, biologists cataloguing Bolivia’s Yungas cloud forest would note a small spotted cat and move on. Tiger cat, broadly speaking. The general profile fit and there was no obvious reason to dig further.

Local communities had always called it something different. Tilcayo, a name that treated this animal as its own thing, not a Bolivian stand-in for something from Brazil.

The DNA backed them up. A study published in Current Biology confirms that the tilcayo, now formally named Leopardus tilcayo, is a species science had never documented. It is the first new living feline to be formally named in more than a century.

Not really a discovery, a correction

The tilcayo has been in Bolivia’s Yungas for a very long time. Genetic analysis puts the split from other tiger cat lineages at about 1.4 million years ago. What changed is not the cat. The tools to study it finally caught up.

“We never expected this Bolivian tiger cat to be a separate species, and no one had ever proposed it as a different animal, subspecies or otherwise,” said Jonas Lescroart, evolutionary biologist at the University of Antwerp and co-lead author of the study.

Tiger cats are what biologists call cryptic species: you cannot tell them apart by looking. You need DNA, and for most of the history of field biology, that was not a practical option. Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, a National Geographic explorer and study co-author, had noticed for years that the Bolivian animals did not match existing descriptions, most of which came from Brazilian populations. That was what prompted the deeper look.

The team analyzed DNA from 38 cats across several South American countries, including eight museum specimens. The result was bigger than the tilcayo alone. Tiger cats are not two species, as currently recognized, but five genetically distinct lineages.

What little is known about the tilcayo

The cat is small, roughly 18 inches (46cm) long and about 3 pounds (1.4kg), lighter than most house cats. Its fur is light brown with irregularly shaped rosettes. Camera traps suggest it is largely nocturnal, and scat samples with rodent remains give some indication of its diet. Beyond that, almost nothing is documented.

Only two live individuals have been examined by the research team. One is a 10-year-old male now at the Senda Verde wildlife sanctuary in Bolivia, where he ended up after years as a household pet with a local family. The rest of what is known comes from camera traps and the animals sampled for the genetic study.

A new species at risk of disappearing

The International Union for Conservation of Nature currently lists tiger cats under two “vulnerable” designations with declining populations. That was assessed without knowing five distinct lineages existed. The research team has shared their findings with the IUCN ahead of its upcoming review, and Lescroart says the tilcayo, assessed on its own, could qualify as endangered.

Its only confirmed habitat is Bolivia’s Yungas forest, one of the most pressured ecosystems in the region. Deforestation, agricultural expansion, fires, and mining are all encroaching. A newly named species with a narrow range, a shrinking home, and almost no population data to go on is a hard situation.

“Showing the general public that even in a flagship group such as cats there are still new species to be discovered may transmit an important message,” said Eduardo Eizirik, evolutionary biologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul and senior author of the study. “There are many undiscovered species out there in the world, and they are at risk of disappearing before we even discover them.”

The tilcayo got a name. That is not nothing. Restoring fire-damaged forest, protecting native cover, and keeping habitat connections intact across the Yungas are the immediate priorities. The question the research leaves open is how many animals like it are still out there, genetically real and ecologically distinct, in places that won’t hold together long enough to be studied.

Source study: Current Biology- Phylogenomics and museomics reveal five distinct species of tiger cats in South America

**Contexto** – Durante años, los biólogos que estudiaban el bosque nuboso de Yungas en Bolivia vieron un pequeño gato manchado y asumieron que era un tipo de gato tigre ya conocido. Sin embargo, las comunidades locales llamaban a este gato “tilcayo”, considerándolo un animal único. Sin herramientas avanzadas, los científicos no se dieron cuenta de que era diferente.

Es la primera nueva especie de gato salvaje identificada en más de 100 años. Los investigadores recolectaron ADN de 38 gatos en Sudamérica y descubrieron que lo que se pensaba que eran dos especies de gatos tigre en realidad son cinco especies distintas.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento muestra que incluso grupos de animales bien conocidos como los gatos aún pueden sorprender a los científicos. El tilcayo es más pequeño y liviano que la mayoría de los gatos domésticos y vive solo en el bosque Yungas de Bolivia, que enfrenta amenazas como la deforestación y la minería. Debido a su hábitat limitado y pequeña población conocida, el tilcayo podría estar en peligro. Este hallazgo impulsa a científicos y conservacionistas a proteger su hábitat antes de que desaparezca.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores compartieron sus hallazgos con grupos de conservación para actualizar el estado de protección del tilcayo. Destacan la necesidad de restaurar los bosques dañados y mantener las conexiones de hábitat en Yungas. Se necesitan más estudios para aprender sobre el comportamiento y el tamaño de la población del tilcayo para ayudar a planificar una conservación efectiva.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Científicos han identificado oficialmente una nueva especie de gato salvaje en el bosque nuboso de Bolivia, destacando la necesidad de proteger su hábitat en disminución y comprender mejor su papel en la naturaleza.
